sourceSentences.text: ‘Many things have been made clear to me this night,’ I said quietly.
I turned to King Shrewd.
‘My lord king, I bid you good evening, and ask to be excused from your presence.’
‘Eh?
So you … had an anxious day, lad?’
‘I did, my lord king,’ I said softly.
His deep eyes looked up into mine as I stood before him, waiting to be released.
I looked deep into their depths.
He was not there.
Not as he once had been.
He looked at me puzzledly, blinked a few times.
‘Well.
Perhaps you had best get some rest then.
As should I. Fool?
Fool, is my bed prepared?
Warm it with the warming pan.
I grow so cold at night these days.
Ha!
At night these days!
There’s a bit of nonsense for you, Fool.
How would you say it, to get it aright?’
The Fool sprang to his feet, bowed deeply before the King.
‘I would say there’s the chill of death about the days these nights as well, your majesty.
A cold fair to curl the bones, it is.
A man could take his death to it.
’Twould warm me more to hide in your shade than to stand before your sun’s heat.’
King Shrewd chuckled.
‘You don’t make a bit of sense, Fool.
But then you never did.
Good night to all, and off to bed, lads, both of you.
Good night, good night.’
I slipped out while Regal was saying a more formal good night to his father.
It was all I could do to walk past Wallace’s simpering smile without smashing it from his face.
Once in the hall outside, I swiftly sought my own room.
I would take the Fool’s advice, I thought, and hide myself in Chade rather than stand before the heat of the King’s son.
I spent the rest of that evening in my room alone.
I knew that as night deepened, Molly would wonder when I did not come tapping at her door.
But I had no heart for it tonight.

I could not summon the energy to slip out of my room and go creeping up the stairs and slinking down the corridors, always worrying that someone might step out abruptly and find me where I had no right to be.
At one time, I would have sought out Molly’s warmth and affection and found a measure of peace there.
That was no longer the case.
Now I dreaded the stealth and anxiety of our meetings, and a guardedness that did not even end when her door closed behind me.
For Verity rode within me, and ever I must guard so that what I felt and thought with Molly did not spill over into the link I shared with Verity.
I gave up on the scroll I had been trying to read.
What use now to learn of Elderlings, anyway?
Verity would find whatever Verity found.
I flung myself back on my bed and stared up at the ceiling.
Even still and silent, there was no peace in me.
My link to Verity was like a hook in my flesh; so must a snagged fish feel when it fights the line.
My ties to Nighteyes were on a deeper, more subtle level, but ever he was there as well, green eyes lambent in a dark corner of myself.
These parts of me never slept, never rested, were never quiescent at all.
And that constant strain was beginning to tell on me.
Hours later, the candles were guttering and the fire burned low.
A change in the air of my room let me know that Chade had opened his soundless door to me.
I arose and went to him.
But with every step I took up that draughty staircase, my anger grew.
It was not the kind of anger that led to ranting and blows between men.
This was an anger born as much from weariness and frustration as from any hurt.
This was the sort of anger that led a man to stop everything, to say simply, ‘I cannot bear this any more.’
‘Cannot bear what?’
Chade asked me.
He looked up from where he hunched over some concoction he was grinding on his stained stone table.
There was genuine concern in his voice.
It made me really stop and look at the man I addressed.
A tall, skinny old assassin.
Pox-scarred.
Hair gone almost entirely white now.
Wearing the familiar grey wool robe, always with stains or the tiny burns he inflicted on his clothes while he worked.
I wondered how many men he had killed for his king, killed simply at a word or nod from Shrewd.
Killed without question, true to his oath.
For all those deaths, he was a gentle man.
Suddenly I had a question, a question more pressing than answering his question.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: I spent the rest of that evening in my room alone. I knew that as night deepened, Molly would wonder when I did not come tapping at her door. But I had no heart for it tonight. I could not summon the energy to slip out of my room and go creeping up the stairs and slinking down the corridors, always worrying that someone might step out abruptly and find me where I had no right to be. At one time, I would have sought out Molly’s warmth and affection and found a measure of peace there. That was no longer the case. Now I dreaded the stealth and anxiety of our meetings, and a guardedness that did not even end when her door closed behind me. For Verity rode within me, and ever I must guard so that what I felt and thought with Molly did not spill over into the link I shared with Verity.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Решту того вечора я провів сам у своїй кімнаті. Я знав, що з настанням ночі Моллі дивуватиметься, чому я не постукав у її двері. Та сьогодні в мене не лежала до цього душа. Я не міг зібрати сил, щоб вислизнути зі своєї кімнати, крадькома піднятися сходами й прослизнути коридорами, весь час побоюючись, що хтось раптом вийде й застане мене там, де я не мав права бути. Колись я шукав тепла й любові Моллі та знаходив там дещицю спокою. Тепер це було не так. Тепер я боявся потайності й тривоги наших зустрічей, і настороженості, що не зникала навіть тоді, коли за мною зачинялися її двері. Бо в мені їхав Веріті, і я мусив повсякчас стерегтися, щоб те, що я відчував і думав з Моллі, не перелилося у зв'язок, який я поділяв з Веріті.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: I gave up on the scroll I had been trying to read. What use now to learn of Elderlings, anyway? Verity would find whatever Verity found. I flung myself back on my bed and stared up at the ceiling. Even still and silent, there was no peace in me. My link to Verity was like a hook in my flesh; so must a snagged fish feel when it fights the line. My ties to Nighteyes were on a deeper, more subtle level, but ever he was there as well, green eyes lambent in a dark corner of myself. These parts of me never slept, never rested, were never quiescent at all. And that constant strain was beginning to tell on me.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Я відклав сувій, який намагався читати. Яка тепер користь дізнаватися про Старших? Веріті знайде те, що знайде Веріті. Я кинувся на ліжко й утупився в стелю. Навіть у нерухомості й мовчанні в мені не було спокою. Мій зв'язок із Веріті був наче гак у плоті; мабуть, так почувається риба, що зачепилася й бореться з волосінню. Мої зв'язки з Нічнооким були глибші й тонші, але й він завжди був там — зелені очі жевріли в темному куточку мене самого. Ці частини мене ніколи не спали, ніколи не відпочивали, узагалі ніколи не були спокійними. І це постійне напруження починало на мені позначатися.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Hours later, the candles were guttering and the fire burned low. A change in the air of my room let me know that Chade had opened his soundless door to me. I arose and went to him. But with every step I took up that draughty staircase, my anger grew. It was not the kind of anger that led to ranting and blows between men. This was an anger born as much from weariness and frustration as from any hurt. This was the sort of anger that led a man to stop everything, to say simply, ‘I cannot bear this any more.’
paragraphPairs.translatedText: За кілька годин свічки вже опливали, а вогонь пригасав. Зміна в повітрі моєї кімнати дала мені зрозуміти, що Чейд відчинив для мене свої беззвучні двері. paragraphPairs.sourceText: ‘Cannot bear what?’ Chade asked me. He looked up from where he hunched over some concoction he was grinding on his stained stone table. There was genuine concern in his voice. It made me really stop and look at the man I addressed. A tall, skinny old assassin. Pox-scarred. Hair gone almost entirely white now. Wearing the familiar grey wool robe, always with stains or the tiny burns he inflicted on his clothes while he worked. I wondered how many men he had killed for his king, killed simply at a word or nod from Shrewd. Killed without question, true to his oath. For all those deaths, he was a gentle man. Suddenly I had a question, a question more pressing than answering his question.

У його голосі бриніла щира тривога. Вона змусила мене справді зупинитися й поглянути на чоловіка, до якого я звертався. Високий, худий старий убивця. У віспяних шрамах. Волосся тепер майже зовсім побіліло. У звичній сірій вовняній одежі, завжди в плямах чи дрібних пропалинах, які він залишав на вбранні під час роботи. Я замислився, скільки людей він убив заради свого короля, убив просто за словом чи кивком Шрюда. Убив без запитань, вірний своїй присязі. Попри всі ці смерті він був лагідною людиною. Раптом у мене виникло питання, нагальніше за відповідь на його питання.
